items.title: EM@3AM: Leadless Cardiac Pacemakers
items.summary: The device you will increasingly find in frail, dialysis-dependent and difficult-access patients, and which behaves nothing like the transvenous pacemaker you were taught on.

_homepage.note: Leadless units are going into exactly the cohort that turns up in your resus bay — frailty, end-stage kidney disease, veins that have already been used up. The piece sets out the complication profile against traditional transvenous devices and closes on a post-implant rhythm question, so it doubles as a short self-test. Short enough to read on a break, specific enough to change what you look for on the chest film.

items.title: Rescuers search for survivors after deadly earthquake in Tibet
items.summary: A magnitude-7 quake near Nagqu with 339 homes down, 12,000 evacuated and more than 5,000 rescuers working through severed communications at altitude.

_homepage.note: Mass-casualty response at 4,500 metres with comms down is a different problem from the same event on a coastal plain, and the reporting carries enough operational detail — collapse counts, evacuation numbers, the scale of the rescue deployment — to be read that way rather than as a disaster headline. Two large quakes off Vanuatu the same day triggered a Pacific tsunami warning, so this is a busy week for the region. The Panama quake coverage in the feed earlier this month is the obvious companion piece.

items.title: Critical Care Evidence Updates, September 2026
items.summary: The month's critical care randomised trials in one pass, including TRICYCLE on multimodal vasopressors in septic shock.

_homepage.note: TRICYCLE sits directly next to the vasopressor material the feed has been accumulating — the ARISE FLUIDS appraisal, the peripheral pressors piece, the VASSPR hot take — and this is the structured, trial-by-trial version of that same argument. The roundup also covers a CRRT protocol trial and sedation with cipepofol versus dexmedetomidine plus propofol. The Bottom Line only posts these monthly, so it is a cheap way to keep the appraisal reading current without chasing journals.

items.title: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro
items.summary: Moonshot's new model benchmarks second only to Claude Opus 5.5, with full weights promised by early November — the open-weight gap closing in public.

_homepage.note: Willison runs it through his own llm tooling rather than reprinting the launch post, which is why his model write-ups are worth reading when the press releases are not. The Artificial Analysis score of 55 against Opus 5.5's 58 is the number to watch: a model that close, released as open weights, changes what can plausibly run on hardware you control. Relevant if any of this is ever going to touch clinical work, where the weights live is not a side issue.

items.title: Labor promises $1.5b to slash Victorian ED wait times
items.summary: A pre-election commitment to expand a dozen emergency departments by 25 per cent, hire 1,500 health workers and add 150 beds — the shape of the system he will be working in next year.

_homepage.note: This lands three weeks after Victorian public hospital doctors walked off the job over a pay dispute that had been stalled for about a year, and the Liberals have countered with $1.3 billion to move public surgical patients into private hospitals. Whichever way the November election goes, one of these two becomes the funding environment for his department. Free to read on ABC, unlike most of the Age's coverage of the same campaign.

items.title: Subnautica 2's next update promises its scariest region yet
items.summary: The next early access drop for Subnautica 2 centres on a large new biome the developers are openly pitching on dread rather than content volume.

_homepage.note: Worth a look in the gap between Enshrouded's 1.0 and Dragonwilds' Luminance update in December — same survival-crafting itch, very different pressure, and the Subnautica series builds its tension out of visibility and air rather than combat. No release date attached yet, so this is advance notice rather than a patch to install. Massively OP stays closer to survival-game roadmaps than the general gaming press does.

items.title: On Fudge, Michael Kiwanuka makes peace with taking his time
items.summary: Kiwanuka's self-produced fourth record, cut alongside Small Changes and delayed by his stroke, reviewed by someone willing to name where the looseness tips into inertia.

_homepage.note: Kiwanuka is already on the shelf, so this is a record to decide about rather than an artist to discover. The review is a 7/10 — it praises the self-production and the string arrangements but argues the freewheeling instinct costs the album momentum across its hour, which is more useful than the uniformly positive notices it collected elsewhere. Out 23 October, which means it will be in Northside and Rocksteady within the fortnight.

items.title: Acute pulmonary edema. Why?
items.summary: A dialysis patient in flash pulmonary oedema whose ECG hides both subendocardial ischaemia and occlusion MI — the exact pairing that gets called 'just heart failure' at 3am.

_homepage.note: The patient arrests after intubation, which makes this a resus case as much as an ECG case: the decision about the cath lab has to be made before the ECG has finished declaring itself. Smith runs it through the Queen of Hearts model, which flags both patterns at once, and the discussion is about what you do when the machine and your own read disagree. Worth sitting with alongside the ACLS arrhythmia pitfalls material already in the feed.

items.title: Fujichrome MS 100/1000 — Irresponsible Pushing
items.summary: A 1999 slide film built to be pushed four stops, shot 27 years expired, with honest results rather than a rescue story.

_homepage.note: Most expired-film writing is either a disaster report or an advertisement; this one is a controlled test of a stock that was actually engineered for the abuse, and the finding — magenta-shifted colour but near-normal reversal contrast — is specific enough to act on. Useful calibration if you have anything old and fast sitting in the fridge. Posted today.

items.title: ACCA Relaunches Landmark NEW26 Emerging Artist Series
items.summary: ACCA's commissioning series for emerging Australian artists returns after nine years, free, and closes 22 November.

_homepage.note: NEW ran from 2003 to 2016 and was how a generation of Australian artists got their first institutional commission; this edition brings back seven of them across painting, film, sculpture and text, and then the series goes biennial. Amanda Bennetts's Axis Mundi on data collection and disability bias, and Diego Ramírez's tarot-and-bureaucracy installation, are the two being singled out. Southbank rather than northside, but free and finite — it ends 22 November.
